title: LANDFALL BAND
subtitle: Wearable sensing concept: annotated block diagram and reference bill of materials

status.text: Block-level concept. No schematic capture, no PCB, never built, never bench-tested. Every current, rate and size here is a design estimate unless its chip says otherwise.
status.why_no_schematic: KiCad was not available during the hackathon, so the deliverable is an annotated block diagram and a reference bill of materials.

principle: The band measures what a wearable can measure. Everything else reaches LANDFALL through a documented interface, drawn as NOT MEASURABLE HERE. It is the same discipline as the software: no number without a source, no measurement without a sensor.
label_rule: Every block carries three labels: (a) the indicator it produces, (b) the LANDFALL rule, baseline or case it feeds, and (c) the NASA requirement that justifies or constrains it.
mfr_basis: Manufacturer specs are quoted only where the manufacturer's own page or datasheet was read for this build (2026-11-14); each block names its source and says whether it was read. The datasheets of five parts (MAX30003, MAX86141, MAX30208, MAX17048, LSM6DSOX) could not be retrieved, so no manufacturer claim is quoted for them: what the design assumes of each part is an open item, and their datasheet URLs are listed for a reviewer.

relations.constraint: limits how this block may be built
relations.analogy: written for another system; the band borrows the pattern and does not claim compliance
relations.delegates: assigns this measurement or alert to another system
relations.reference: NASA page that names the measurement (not a requirement)

gap.claim: No operational wearable sensor specification: the ExMC Mars medical concept of operations assumes the crew wears biosensors and specifies none.
gap.detail: Its emergency-care scenario assumes "All crewmembers are wearing biosensors", and its narratives warn that "Specific technologies are only representative and are not intended to indicate requirements": no sensor, sampling rate or performance is given. NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev F has no wearable or biosensor requirement (declared below). NASA's Spaceflight Standard Measures is a research study that collects "a standardized set of measurements", including activity and light from a wrist sensor; it is not an operational sensor specification. The band is one concrete, cited proposal for that gap.
gap.doc: Urbina M, McGuire K, Lehnhardt K, Fleming N. Medical System Concept of Operations for Mars Exploration Mission-11. NASA HRP Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC) Element, HRP-48021, Baseline April 2019
gap.verified_in: the NTRS full text, read 2026-11-14; not frozen in this build

heart.title: Heart signals: one continuous, one on demand

points.head: Continuous: optical pulse (PPG)
points.text: The optical sensor under the band reads the pulse around the clock. Its pulse inter-beat intervals give heart rate and, in sleep, the resting heart rate and the variability indicator. Variability computed from pulse intervals is pulse-rate variability (PRV), an approximation of heart-rate variability (HRV): close at rest, poor in motion, so the band computes it only in low-motion sleep.

points.head: On demand: single-lead ECG
points.text: An ECG needs a lead across the heart, and two electrodes on one wrist cannot form one. The band's ECG records only while a finger of the other hand touches its outer electrode, which closes an arm-to-arm lead like limb lead I, for a 30-s strip. It cannot run while the band is simply worn, so no indicator comes from it.

flown_reference.name: CSA Bio-Monitor (Hexoskin Astroskin)
facts: A garment, not a wristband: NASA's ISS report calls the Bio-Monitor "a wearable garment capable of monitoring relevant physiological parameters for up to 48 hours"; CSA astronaut David Saint-Jacques' 48-hour recording session was debriefed on 2019-02-28.
Astroskin "consists of a shirt-based garment and headband with embedded sensors", among them a 3-lead ECG in the shirt.
Tested in NASA's HERA Campaign 3 (four 30-day missions, 16 crewmembers), a test that "will elevate the TRL from 5 to 6".
Recorder: two replaceable AA batteries for 48 hours of autonomy, 400+ hours of local raw data storage, Bluetooth 2.1, 62 × 78 × 23 mm, 75 g without batteries.
Exports JSON, CSV, EDF and binary (synchronous channels as RIFF/WAV); timestamps count 256ths of a second.
flown_reference.basis: Read on 2026-11-14 in the public sources listed with it; not frozen in this build.

sources.label: Toscano W, Cowings P, Sullivan P, et al. Wearable Biosensor Monitor to Support Autonomous Crew Health and Readiness to Perform. NASA HRP Investigators' Workshop, 2017. NTRS 20190001996
Hexoskin API documentation, datatype registry (channel rates, PTT, Nonin delay)
Hexoskin API documentation, data resource (export formats, 65,536-value cap)
Hexoskin API documentation (timestamps in 256ths of a second)

over the last 300 s (LF and HF by Lomb periodogram)

anchors.quote: Assessing, recording, monitoring, and trending vital signs and additional physiological and behavioral health signs.
anchors.why: The root requirement for the whole product: in-mission medical capability includes monitoring and trending vital signs.

anchors.quote: Periodic monitoring of general health status.
anchors.why: In-mission preventive care includes periodic monitoring: the band is the periodic, passive part of it.

anchors.quote: Medical equipment shall be usable by non-physician crewmembers in the event that a physician crewmember is not present or is the one who requires medical treatment.
anchors.why: No settings to tune: the band has no screen and no calibration step. The crew wears it and docks it to charge; the only action it asks for is an ECG spot check, one finger on the outer electrode for 30 s.

anchors.quote: The system shall allow the crewmember to effectively input, store, receive, display, process, distribute, update, monitor and dispose of relevant information on consumable levels, suit status and alerts, and biomedical data.
anchors.why: Written for suits. It is the nearest NASA text on a worn system that handles biomedical data; its rationale asks for real-time heart rhythm and derived core temperature.
anchors.note: Not cited: [V2 11034], [V2 11035] and [V2 11036] (record, display and alert) are about suit pressure, ppO2 and ppCO2, the suited atmosphere. They are not biomedical or wearable requirements, so the band claims nothing from them.

anchors.quote: The system shall provide visual indication when a data parameter is stale, missing, unavailable, or unknown.
anchors.why: The band reports off-wrist time and the age of its last sync, so LANDFALL can mark band data STALE or MISSING instead of showing a value that is not current.

blocks.name: Optical pulse (PPG): HR, PRV, SpO2
blocks.function: Optical front end and the band's heart-rate source: red and infrared LEDs and a photodiode under a window on the inner face. The infrared pulse channel runs around the clock, and its pulse inter-beat intervals give heart rate and, in sleep, pulse-rate variability. Red and infrared together give SpO2 in spot windows.

datasheet.note: Not retrieved for this build. The number of optical channels and LED drivers is unverified, so none is claimed here.

source.arithmetic: Bio-Monitor PPG 64 Hz, kept at 64 Hz
Bio-Monitor HRV over 300 s, kept at 300 s (5-min windows)
Bio-Monitor SpO2 1 Hz, kept at 1 Hz

source.rationale: LED current dominates the power budget, so only the infrared pulse channel runs continuously; the red LED joins it for SpO2 in windows (10 % duty).

produces.label: Resting heart rate
produces.how: lowest stable 5-min heart rate in the main sleep period, from pulse inter-beat intervals

produces.label: Heart rate variability (SDNN), measured as PRV
produces.how: SDNN of pulse inter-beat intervals in 5-min windows of low-motion sleep, averaged over the night: pulse-rate variability (PRV), an approximation of HRV, not ECG-derived HRV

produces.label: Heart rate, 1-min means
produces.how: mean pulse rate in each 1-min epoch, around the clock; shown on Trends as context, and no rule reads it

produces.label: SpO2 (spot windows)
produces.how: recorded and shown as context; no LANDFALL rule uses it

feeds.as: reliable change vs own baseline: PRV against a PRV baseline
NASA-STD-3001 publishes no numeric in-flight alert thresholds for crew health; its alert requirements leave the number to the program. LANDFALL invents none for SpO2

justified_by.quote: Assessing, recording, monitoring, and trending vital signs and additional physiological and behavioral health signs.

For equipment such as bioinstrumentation and medical devices, that are specifically designed to contact the human body, electrical leakage currents caused by contact with exposed surfaces (including in worst-case fault scenarios) shall be kept below the levels specified in Table 9.3-11
justified_by.note: The optical window is not an electrode, but the band as a whole is bioinstrumentation on intact skin, so its total leakage is held to the External rows of Table 9.3-11 (see the ECG block).

justified_by.quote: Any surface to which the bare skin of the crew is exposed shall not cause skin temperature to enter the range for pain/injury in Table 9.3-5
justified_by.note: The pulse LED runs around the clock against the skin, so this limit applies all day, not only in spot windows.

limits.rationale: 2 °C below the start of the Table 9.3-5 pain range; read from the skin temperature sensors.

design: Pulse-rate variability is not heart-rate variability: pulse intervals also carry the beat-to-beat variation of the pulse's travel time from heart to wrist. So the band computes hrv_sdnn only in low-motion sleep, labels it PRV, and Tier B compares it only with the crewmember's own PRV baseline, never with ECG-derived norms (see the published basis).
Pulse intervals are kept only from epochs the accelerometer scores as low-motion. Daytime heart rate in motion is a trend for Trends, not an indicator.

Timing resolution: at 64 Hz one sample is 15.6 ms, so peak-time quantization adds an interval error of 15.625 / √6 = 6.4 ms (SD). On an illustrative SDNN of 50 ms that gives √(50² + 6.4²) = 50.4 ms, a 0.4 ms bias that is the same in the crewmember's own baseline; peak interpolation shrinks it further.
Each sample is timestamped at acquisition on the MCU clock and the AFE's fixed pipeline delay is written in the log header, never assumed to be zero (see the Nonin 172 ms pitfall).

evidence.claim: PRV is an acceptable estimate of HRV at rest, but not in motion.
evidence.quote: Results speak in favor of sufficient accuracy when subjects are at rest, although many studies suggest that short-term variability is somewhat overestimated by PRV, which reflects coupling effects between respiration and the cardiovascular system. Physical activity and some mental stressors seem to impair the agreement of PRV and HRV, often to an inacceptable extent.

source.citation: Schäfer A, Vagedes J. How accurate is pulse rate variability as an estimate of heart rate variability? A review on studies comparing photoplethysmographic technology with an electrocardiogram. Int J Cardiol 2013;166(1):15-29. doi:10.1016/j.ijcard.2012.03.119. PMID 22809539

blocks.name: Spot ECG: finger of other hand
blocks.function: Single-lead ECG front end for an on-demand spot check. One dry electrode on the inner face rests on the wrist; a second on the outer face is touched by a finger of the other hand, which closes a lead from one arm to the other, across the chest, like limb lead I. Two electrodes on one wrist have no lead across the heart, so the ECG records only during a spot check, never while the band is simply worn.

datasheet.note: Not retrieved for this build. Sample width, on-chip R-R detection and the 256 sps setting are unverified, so none is claimed here.

source.arithmetic: Bio-Monitor ECG 256 Hz, kept at 256 sps

source.rationale: Long enough for a rhythm strip the crewmember can hold still for. It is also the session length of the FDA-authorized watch ECG in the published basis (DEN180044).

produces.label: ECG spot check: 30-s single-lead strip
produces.how: recorded only on demand, while the other hand touches the outer electrode; stored raw on the band for the Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon (no viewer yet: open item)

feeds.as: LANDFALL reads no ECG: no rule uses the strip and nothing classifies its rhythm

justified_by.quote: Conducting ancillary tests as needed, including imaging (e.g., cardiac, vascular, ocular), laboratory analyses, and electrocardiography.

For equipment such as bioinstrumentation and medical devices, that are specifically designed to contact the human body, electrical leakage currents caused by contact with exposed surfaces (including in worst-case fault scenarios) shall be kept below the levels specified in Table 9.3-11
justified_by.note: Table 9.3-11 splits body contact into External and Internal. The electrodes touch intact skin only, so LANDFALL reads the External rows (our reading: the table does not name wrist devices). During a spot check the current path runs from one arm to the other, across the chest. The rationale names electrocardiogram (ECG) monitors as isolated equipment; isolated and non-isolated equipment share the External values, and the rationale says the sum of all leakage currents is what counts. General body-current limits for any equipment are [V2 9019] to [V2 9021] (see Safety constraints).

limits.what: Leakage, External body contact, DC to 1 kHz, normal condition
Leakage, External body contact, DC to 1 kHz, single fault

justified_by.quote: Derived body core temperature and heart rhythm (real-time) are desired for microgravity operations
justified_by.note: From the rationale; written for suits. A 30-s spot check is not real-time rhythm monitoring: that needs electrodes across the chest, as in the flown Bio-Monitor's shirt.

design: The inner electrode touches the wrist around the clock, so the Table 9.3-11 footnote applies: "*For DC, there is a small risk of heating and tissue necrosis for prolonged duration of contact." A current path through the body exists only while the other hand closes the circuit; the front end is powered down between spot checks, and every DC lead-bias and lead-off current must still be checked against the footnote (open item).

Each spot check also logs the PPG pulse intervals of the same beats, so pulse timing can be compared with R-R intervals for this crewmember at rest: about 30 beats, a sanity check, not a validation of nightly PRV.
Raw waveforms are kept only for spot checks: the 4 MiB ring holds 182 of them (see the log arithmetic).
The band does not estimate blood pressure from ECG-to-PPG transit time (see the Bio-Monitor pitfalls).

evidence.claim: The same electrode arrangement in an FDA-authorized wrist ECG: electrodes on the back touch the wrist, a finger touches the crown, 30 s, a single lead similar to lead I.
evidence.quote: The watch also contains electrodes on the back of the device which are in continuous contact with the user’s wrist. The watch acquires the electrical potential between the electrodes and digital crown.

source.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. De Novo classification request for ECG App (DEN180044), Apple Inc., De Novo date August 14, 2018: decision summary

nRF52840: CPU duty, pulse detection, BLE sync, clock
MAX30003: powered down between 30-s spot checks

steps.rationale: Nothing here has been measured; doubling is our hedge.

steps.rationale: One whole case tripwire window on one charge: cases.json reassess_after_s = 259,200 s (72 h) for renal_stone and sleep_circadian.

power.comparison: The flown Bio-Monitor runs 48 h on two AA batteries while it records 3-lead ECG at 256 Hz, respiration at 128 Hz and continuous PPG from a shirt and headband. The band records fewer channels on purpose, and its ECG only on demand.
power.no_requirement: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev F sets no battery-endurance requirement for wearables: its three mentions of batteries are about other things. The 72 h target is ours.

steps.label: Pulse inter-beat intervals at 100 bpm, 2 B each
steps.arithmetic: 100 beats/min × 1,440 min × 2 B = 288,000 B/day (the pulse channel runs around the clock; 100 bpm is a deliberately high planning rate: design choice)

steps.label: 1-min epoch records, 32 B each
steps.arithmetic: 1,440 epochs × 32 B = 46,080 B/day (activity, motion flag, 1-min heart rate, light bands, 2 skin temperatures, SpO2 window, flags, MET: design choice)

steps.label: Log depth target
steps.rationale: One whole Tier B baseline window: personal.json rci.baseline_window_days = 14. A lost tablet does not cost anyone their baseline.

steps.label: Raw ECG rate during a spot check
steps.arithmetic: 256 samples/s × 3 B per stored sample = 768 B/s (3 B per sample is a design choice; the front end's sample width is not verified in this build)

steps.label: Spot checks the ring holds
steps.arithmetic: 5,461 s / 30 s = 182 spot checks of 30 s

steps.label: Raw PPG rate, pulse channel
steps.arithmetic: 64 samples/s × 3 B per stored sample = 192 B/s (3 B per sample is a design choice; the front end's sample width is not verified in this build)

steps.label: Raw PPG if the whole flash held it
steps.arithmetic: 16,777,216 B / 192 B/s = 87,381 s = 24.3 h. This is why the band logs pulse inter-beat intervals, not the optical waveform.

not_measurable_here.what: Urine output and fluid intake (24 h)
not_measurable_here.why: No wearable measures urine volume or what a crewmember drinks.

Two systems outside the band do this. The vehicle's radiation monitoring system raises the radiation alarm and reports dose rate ([V2 6164]); [V2 6165] asks the program to monitor the space weather outside the vehicle, proton flux spectra included, which takes an external space-weather monitor outside the shielding. Organ dose in mGy-Eq needs those detectors and the ground's models. The band measures none of these, and LANDFALL is not the radiation alarm: it opens the health case that follows and guides the crew. In the Mars scenario the flux comes from an external monitor in Mars orbit that reports one ≥10 MeV integral channel, not the spectra (the shelter case lists the proton spectrum as not measurable here), relayed locally with no Earth link (continuous relay is a scenario assumption); its values replay the real GOES-7 record of October 1989 with no distance or atmospheric correction (a scenario assumption).
not_measurable_here.via: Vehicle radiation monitor (alarm, dose); external space-weather monitor (proton flux)

requirement.quote: The radiation monitoring system shall alert the crew and operations teams when radiation exposure rates exceed predefined thresholds.
requirement.note: Its rationale: "The crew must be alerted even if ground communication is disrupted or is unviable."

also.quote: The program shall monitor the in-situ extravehicular space weather environment including the external exposure rates, electron flux spectra, and proton flux spectra.
also.note: Its rationale names the storms LANDFALL's scenario draws on: "Historically significant space weather storming includes the August 1972 and October 1989 events." The SPE case replays the real GOES-7 record of October 1989.

examples.name: OSDR Inspiration4 panels
examples.text: real per-subject reference ranges, measured before and after flight only

not_measurable_here.why: Neither is a wrist measurement here. Wrist transit-time methods give systolic only and need per-user adjustment (see the Bio-Monitor pitfalls), and glucose needs a drop of blood. Both are measured with the vehicle medical kit, a cuff and a fingerstick glucometer, and entered by hand. NASA-STD-3001 sets no numeric limit for either (Vol 1 Rev C and Vol 2 Rev F print no blood-pressure or glucose number), so LANDFALL compares each reading only with the crewmember's own baseline (Tier B, caution at most).
not_measurable_here.via: Vehicle medical kit: cuff and fingerstick glucometer, entered by hand

negatives.claim: No EMI/EMC requirement exists in NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev F.
negatives.detail: The only electromagnetic requirement is human RF exposure, [V2 6102]. Citing a [V2] number for EMC would be fabrication; EMC qualification comes from the program.

negatives.claim: No skin-contact biocompatibility requirement exists in Vol 2 Rev F.
negatives.detail: Nearest: [V2 7076] clothing comfort and composition, and [V2 7081] microbiologically safe surfaces; material assessment is deferred to NASA-STD-6016.

negatives.claim: No wearable or biosensor requirement in Vol 2 Rev F.
negatives.detail: The search finds no wearable, biosensor or body-worn device anywhere in the volume. The ExMC Mars medical concept of operations (NTRS 20200001715) assumes "All crewmembers are wearing biosensors" and specifies none: no sensor list, rate or performance.

negatives.claim: No battery-endurance requirement for wearables in Vol 2 Rev F.
negatives.detail: Vol 2 Rev F mentions batteries 3 times, about traverse power projection and maintenance, never endurance. The autonomy target is a design choice.

negatives.claim: No storage-capacity, retention or log-duration requirement in Vol 2 Rev F.
negatives.detail: Zero hits for storage capacity, retention or log duration. The log-depth target is a design choice.
negatives.pattern: data storage|storage capacity|data retention|retention period|log duration|logging duration

pitfalls.title: Its blood pressure is systolic-only and PTT-derived
pitfalls.text: The Bio-Monitor's blood pressure is not a cuff reading. Its registry lists systolic pressure only, "derived from the PTT value" (the pulse transit time between the ECG QRS and the PPG), in a raw form and in a form "Adjusted for user specs".
pitfalls.consequence: The band does not estimate blood pressure. Blood pressure is measured with the cuff in the vehicle medical kit and entered by hand: a hand-off.

pitfalls.title: The Nonin sensor adds a 172 ms delay
pitfalls.text: The registry warns that "The Nonin PPG digital output is delayed by 172 ms", which must be subtracted when computing pulse transit time, and that the PPG channel "is not exactly aligned with the other channels (~0.05 s delay)".
pitfalls.consequence: Every band channel is timestamped at acquisition on one clock, and each front end's fixed delay is written in the log header.

pitfalls.title: CSV and JSON exports cap at 65,536 values per datatype
pitfalls.text: "For JSON and CSV formats, the result size is constrained to 65536 values per datatype": about 18 h at 1 Hz, so high-rate channels need the binary path.
pitfalls.consequence: Pulse inter-beat intervals at 100 bpm reach 65,536 values in 10.9 h, so they leave the band in binary records; 1-min epochs would take 45.5 days to reach the cap.

pitfalls_basis: Hexoskin's public API documentation (datatype registry and data resource), read 2026-11-14; not frozen in this build.

safety.topic: Leakage current, medical and bioinstrumentation equipment
safety.text: The band touches intact skin, read as External body contact: DC to 1 kHz, 0.1 mA normal and 0.5 mA single fault, the sum of all leakage currents. Footnote: prolonged DC contact carries a small risk of heating and tissue necrosis. The two ECG electrodes are the band's only conductive contacts: the inner one rests on the wrist, and a path across the chest exists only while the other hand touches the outer one during a spot check.

safety.topic: Current through the crewmember, general limits for any equipment
safety.text: Nominal contact with conductive housing: 0.4 mA DC, 0.2 mA peak AC. Startle reaction, during critical operations: 2 mA DC, 0.5 mA AC. Catastrophic, all circumstances: 40 mA DC, 8 mA peak AC. For bioinstrumentation the stricter [V2 9023] applies.
The crew must be able to interrupt power and see the de-energized status. The band has no switch or status light in this BOM: an open item.

Tissue damage at 49 °C or above (Table 9.3-4); pain range 43 to 49 °C (Table 9.3-5). The LEDs stop at 41 °C at the skin-side sensor (design choice); the pulse LED runs around the clock, so the cut-off is always armed.
The BLE radio must keep crew RF exposure within Table 6.8-2. This is the only electromagnetic requirement in Vol 2.

Non-Critical: under 4 Wh per isolated pack, Li-ion COTS up to 1000 mAh. Critical: single-fault tolerant, Li-ion COTS under 20 V and 60 Wh. Catastrophic: two-fault tolerant. Section 4.4.3: monitor cell voltage, cell temperature and current.

links.label: NASA-STD-6001B in the NASA Technical Standards System

safety.text: Test 1 upward flame propagation (five specimens of 30 × 6.5 cm; none may burn more than 15 cm), Test 4 electrical wire insulation flammability, Test 7 offgassed products (72 ± 1 h at 50 ± 3 °C; total T value below 0.5), Test 18 arc tracking. A material that is untested or fails these tests needs a Materials Usage Agreement (MUA) under NASA-STD-6016.

safety_basis: Vol 2 Rev F items are frozen in std_vol2_requirements. JSC-20793 Rev D (NTRS 20170009182) and NASA-STD-6001B w/Change 3 are public NASA documents, not frozen in this build; their numbers here were checked against them on 2026-11-14.
open_items: No schematic capture or PCB: block level only (KiCad not available).
Every current in the power budget is an estimate; bench measurement replaces it.

Battery monitoring: the MCP73831 has no thermistor input (verified on its datasheet) and the MAX17048's current and temperature measurement is not verified, so JSC-20793 section 4.4.3 is treated as not met. Fix: a gauge whose datasheet shows current and temperature measurement.

Five datasheets were not read in this build (MAX30003, MAX86141, MAX30208, MAX17048, LSM6DSOX): confirm each part offers what the design assumes (256 sps ECG, a continuous low-power pulse channel plus an SpO2 mode, an accelerometer rate of 52 Hz, skin-range accuracy, I2C addressing) before selection.
PRV against ECG: measure how far the band's pulse-interval SDNN departs from ECG SDNN in sleep; until then hrv_sdnn is compared only with the crewmember's own PRV baseline.
Pulse wavelength: the design reuses the SpO2 infrared LED for the continuous pulse channel; choose the wavelength on the bench.
No ECG viewer: LANDFALL does not show the spot-check strip to the Crew Medical Officer or put it in the ground packet yet.
Confirm two TWI (I2C) instances on the nRF52840 beside SPI and QSPI in its product specification: the design uses two I2C buses.
Prolonged DC contact: check every DC lead-bias and lead-off current of the ECG front end against Table 9.3-11 and its footnote, with the front end powered down between spot checks.
No power switch or status light for [V2 9017] / [V2 9018].
Power tree (front-end and LED supply rails) not designed.
Electrode material, strap and housing materials not selected: NASA-STD-6001B testing or a Materials Usage Agreement is needed.
Core body temperature is not derived: that needs a validated model.
Check the MAX30208 addressing on the datasheet before layout; the two-bus split avoids the question for now.
build_notes: Five part datasheets (MAX30003, MAX86141, MAX30208, MAX17048, LSM6DSOX) are hosted on analog.com and st.com, which did not answer automated downloads during the build on 2026-11-14. Manufacturer claims drafted for those parts earlier were removed rather than kept unverified.

The Bio-Monitor channel table, pitfalls and recorder facts were first transcribed before the hackathon from Hexoskin's documentation. On 2026-11-14 each was re-read on the public pages listed with the flown reference, and three were corrected: the recorder runs on replaceable AA batteries (its product page says it "is not rechargeable"); HERA Campaign 3 was a test meant to raise the TRL from 5 to 6, not a validation at that level; and the registry gives the systolic estimate at 1 Hz, so it is no longer called non-continuous.

JSC-20793 Rev D and NASA-STD-6001B w/Change 3 were first read before the hackathon. On 2026-11-14 their numbers were re-checked in the public copies linked under Safety constraints, and the battery quotes were replaced by the documents' verbatim text.

The ExMC Mars concept of operations (NTRS 20200001715), the PRV review (PMID 22809539) and the FDA De Novo summary DEN180044 were read in full text on 2026-11-14. None is frozen in this build, so the band test cannot re-check those quotes; each one links to its source.

An earlier draft put two ECG electrodes on the inner face and took resting heart rate and HRV from their R-R intervals. Two electrodes on one wrist form no lead across the heart, so that could not work: heart rate and HRV now come from the optical pulse, and the ECG is an on-demand spot check closed by the other hand.
